tip: SWARF MACHINING — 5-axis strategy that machines by the TOOL SIDE (not bottom) where the CONTACT AREA between tool + workpiece is a LINE (not a point). FUNDAMENTAL ADVANTAGE: traditional point-contact toolpaths (ball mill stepping across a wall) require many small passes; SWARF cuts the WHOLE WALL HEIGHT in a SINGLE PASS. PHYSICAL principle: the tool side (full flute length) PRESSES AGAINST the wall + sweeps along it; line-contact = much MORE MATERIAL REMOVED per unit time + far BETTER SURFACE QUALITY (no scallop pattern from multiple stepdown passes). PRIMARY USE CASE: STEEP AREAS (walls near-vertical to the table). Per h3d24-005 shallow-area strategy works on flat-ish surfaces; SWARF complements it for the steep complement. SWARF + HSR/HSM rough + HSM finish are the canonical 3-pass aerospace 5-axis workflow (per ic24-XXX 5-axis sim).

SWARF vs TRADITIONAL STEEP-AREA MACHINING — order-of-magnitude pass-count + cycle-time difference. EXAMPLE: 50mm-tall vertical wall, 6mm cutter. TRADITIONAL Constant Z (per h3d24-002): step down by 0.5mm each pass → 100 passes; each pass traverses the wall length. SWARF: SINGLE PASS along the wall with tool-side fully engaged → 1 pass instead of 100; cycle time ~100× faster on this specific feature. ALSO BETTER FINISH: traditional 100 passes leaves a scalloped surface (visible step marks at each Z-level); SWARF leaves a SMOOTH LINE-CONTACT FINISH equivalent to a perfectly continuous cut. CAVEAT: requires 5-AXIS SIMULTANEOUS (tool axis must continuously match wall normal); requires a tool whose side profile MATCHES the wall geometry (straight tapered for straight walls, contoured tool for contoured walls). LIMITATIONS: doesn't work on horizontal surfaces (point contact needed there); doesn't work on inside corners smaller than tool diameter (geometric impossibility).

AEROSPACE 5-AXIS 3-PASS WORKFLOW — canonical sequence for complex parts (turbine blades, impellers, blisks, structural ribs): (1) HSR (High Speed Roughing) — rapid bulk material removal via iMachining or 3D HSR Contour Roughing; large tool, conservative engagement, leaves stock for finishing (~0.5-2mm). (2) HSM SEMI-FINISH — smaller tool, evenly removes the HSR stock leftover; leaves 0.05-0.2mm for finish. (3) SWARF FINISHING (or 5-axis Sim) — line-contact final cut; tool side fully engaged on the steep walls; achieves design surface finish in single pass per feature. CYCLE-TIME ALLOCATION: typically HSR=60-70%, HSM semi-finish=20-25%, SWARF finish=5-15% of total. SURFACE-FINISH ALLOCATION: HSR irrelevant (will be re-cut), HSM gets close, SWARF achieves the final spec. SWITCHING ORDER (HSR after SWARF, etc) = catastrophic — SWARF expects clean prior surface; rough-after-SWARF wastes the SWARF investment. TUTORIAL example: aerospace bracket with HSR Contour roughing → HSM combined finish → SWARF on the steep aerospace contour walls.

source.author: SolidCAM (Autodesk OEM)
source.section: HSR + HSM + iMachining + SWARF Semi-Finish + SWARF Finish

tip: SWARF TOOL SELECTION — pick by GEOMETRY MATCH to the wall being SWARF-cut: (1) STRAIGHT VERTICAL WALL — STANDARD SQUARE-END END MILL (with flute length ≥ wall height); tool side perpendicular to floor. (2) ANGLED WALL (constant draft) — TAPERED END MILL matching the wall draft angle; tool flute side aligns parallel to wall. (3) CONTOURED WALL (changing curvature) — SPECIAL CONTOURED PROFILE tool OR Sim 5-Axis with constantly-changing tool orientation. (4) BALL-NOSE — works but WASTE the tool's tip capability (only the side engages); use square or tapered if available. FLUTE LENGTH REQUIREMENT: tool must have flute extending the FULL wall height OR exceed it; partial-flute coverage = banded surface finish (parts of wall cut by flute, parts cut by smooth shank). CARBIDE preferred over HSS for SWARF — line-contact heat load is concentrated; HSS dulls fast. JM Die rule for SWARF: dedicated SWARF-tool inventory (separate from general-purpose end mills) maintained with verified flute geometry + sharpness.

source.author: SolidCAM (Autodesk OEM)
source.section: HSR and HSM Operations — Tool selection

tip: SWARF MACHINING REQUIRES 5-AXIS SIMULTANEOUS — the tool axis must CONTINUOUSLY match the WALL NORMAL as the toolpath sweeps; this requires simultaneous X+Y+Z+A+B (or +C) motion. CANNOT be done on 3-axis or 3+2-axis machines (those would require multiple setups + faceted approximation that loses SWARF's line-contact benefit). TUTORIAL example machine: FANUC5X_HEAD — head-table 5-axis configuration per ic24-003 kinematics; spindle tilts (A or B head axis) + rotates (C axis) while X/Y/Z linear positions. HEAD-TYPE vs TABLE-TYPE for SWARF: HEAD-TYPE preferred for large/heavy workpieces (table doesn't move = stability); TABLE-TYPE acceptable for smaller workpieces. CONTROLLER REQUIREMENT: must support smooth 5-axis interpolation (Heidenhain TNC, Fanuc 30i+, Siemens 840D); legacy controllers without rotational tool-tip compensation (RTCP / TCPM) cannot run SWARF correctly. POST-PROCESSOR must emit RTCP-aware code to map machine kinematics to programmed tool-axis vectors.

SWARF AEROSPACE USE CASES — the strategy is DOMINANT in aerospace 5-axis work because aerospace structural parts have many steep contoured walls: (1) TURBINE BLADES — airfoil profiles with steep contoured walls along blade leading/trailing edges. (2) IMPELLER VANES — radial pump/compressor vanes with twisted-contour faces. (3) BLISKS (BLaded dISKs) — integrated bladed disk where each blade is SWARF-cut from a solid disk billet. (4) STRUCTURAL RIBS — aircraft fuselage/wing internal ribs with tall thin walls; SWARF preserves wall straightness vs traditional pass-stepping. (5) MOLD CAVITIES with steep walls — SWARF for the steep sections, ball-mill HSM for the rest. (6) MEDICAL implants (e.g., spinal cages with steep features). KEY PROPERTY across all uses: the parts have CONSTRAINTS that favor SWARF — surface finish demand + thin walls (chatter risk with traditional stepping) + complex contoured walls. WAIVERS — non-aerospace 'simple' parts (rectangular pockets, prismatic bosses) don't need SWARF; ROI is in the aerospace-class precision/finish/material-removal-rate combination.

SWARF DRIVE FACES — the operator-selected faces that DRIVE the tool axis. WORKFLOW: (1) Constraint boundaries → Selected faces → Boundary name → Define in Drive faces section. (2) PICK FROM MODEL → click each face to SWARF-cut. (3) FIND FACES button can auto-extend selection to similar adjacent faces (e.g., all faces with same draft angle). KEY CONCEPT: each drive face's NORMAL drives the tool-axis orientation when the tool is cutting that face; transitioning between faces requires smooth tool-axis interpolation (auto-handled by 5-axis post). BOUNDARY-TOOL RELATION options: CENTERED (tool axis runs along center of wall thickness — most common); INSIDE/OUTSIDE (tool axis offset to inner or outer edge — for asymmetric walls). OFFSET parameter (e.g., 2mm in tutorial) leaves stock for finishing OR provides safety margin. ERROR PATTERN: selecting WRONG face set (e.g., a flat-top instead of a steep-wall) → SWARF generates erratic tool motion; verify selection in 3D preview before generation.

InventorCAM iMACHINING DATABASE — SolidCAM/InventorCAM's PROPRIETARY HSM TUNING DATABASE that drives auto-F+S for iMachining 2D/3D + informs related strategies (SWARF + 3D HSM). 3 KEY PARAMETERS: (1) MACHINE — operator defines a machine in the database with HP, max spindle RPM, axis acceleration, table size, rigidity rating. (2) MATERIAL — operator defines workpiece material with HRc hardness, ISO classification, machinability rating. (3) MACHINING LEVEL — slider 1-10 representing aggressiveness; LEVEL 1 = ultra-conservative (long tool life, slow MRR); LEVEL 10 = MAX aggressive (high MRR, faster tool wear); LEVEL 6 = TUTORIAL DEFAULT (balanced). The database CROSS-REFERENCES these 3 to auto-compute F+S, stepover, stepdown, engagement angle. ECONOMIC NOTE: iMachining license is SEPARATE from base InventorCAM ($$$); the database is the differentiator. ANALOGOUS to: Mastercam Dynamic Mill internal tuning (less exposed to operator); hyperMILL Optimised Roughing scallop-driven param (hm18-002 — different UX, same goal).
